info.name: 1. openEHR REST APIs
info.description:
This is a collection of API calls provided as part of the [Apperta C4H Platform](https://platfrom.code4health.org) which represent two common openEHR REST APIs - the Better Ehrscape API and the official openEHR REST API.

The collection is designed to run in parallel with Apperta C4H Platform Postman Environments, which supply the appropriate baseURLs and authentication variables. In some cases, environment variables are automatically updated by the results of requests.

- The official [openEHR REST API specifications](https://specifications.openehr.org/releases/ITS-REST/latest/index.html)
    

are gradually superseding various similar vendor-specific REST APIs. This is currently supported by Better, DIPS, Code24 and ehrBase.

The `openehrBaseURL` environment variable is used to point to the openEHR REST API endpoint of the CDR, if this is supported, otherwise this will be `null`.

- The proprietary [Better Ehrscape API](https://www.ehrscape.com/api-explorer.html), is also largely supported by EhrBase and some other CDRs.
    

It includes some API calls which are currently only supported by Better but is broadly aligned to the official openEHR REST API.

The `ehrscapeBaseURL` environment variable is used to point to the Ehrscape REST API endpoint of the CDR, if this is supported, otherwise this will be `null`.

## Environment

The [workspace](https://www.postman.com/freshehr/freshehr-openehr-apis/overview) that contains this collection also provides an [enviroment](https://www.postman.com/freshehr/freshehr-openehr-apis/environment/44592442-0b6866a2-ed0b-4138-8cc5-fad36cfdc9a8) that has usefull variables for running ehrBASE in docker on a local machine.

## Authorization

By default, authorization is disabled. Since this is the default behaviour when starting ehrBASE using the docker compose in it's git repo. Variables can be enabled that align with the default username and password in case ehrbase is started with 'basic' authentication instead of 'none'.

Other CDRs may have slightly different approaches to authorization.

### Better/ EhrBase

Better and EHrBase CDRs use a Basic Auth string passed via the `Authorization` header, which also acts as a route to the appropriate CDR domain in multiple-domain CDRs such as the Apperta C4H platform. Basic Auth would normally only be used for development and testing, with something like Bearer Token Authorisation used in production.

item.name: A. Tutorial
Check the CDR connections

request.description:
This call will fetch a list of openEHR Templates currently registered on the CDR via the openEHR REST API.

If the CDR connection is working correctly, you should get a response code of `201` or `204` (if there are no templates).

If you do get an error, check that the `openehrBaseUrl`, `Username` and `Password` environment variables are correct.

response.name: Check the openEHR REST connection

request.description:
openEHR templates are aggregations of logical archetype models that along with the basic Reference model, act as the validation schema for any patient data submitted to the CDR. 

You cannot submit any information to a CDR without first registering the template which will be used to validate it.

This section will test our connection to the CDR by running a `GET /template` call.

#### Response

A successful call will return `200` and a list of registered templates.

### Troubleshooting

If you are unable to retrieve the list of templates, ensure that you are using the correct URL for the endpoint, and the correct `Authorization` header for your chosen CDR.

If you are working within Postman, make sure that you have a valid Environment loaded as the collection uses that to set the correct `Username` and `Password` variables to generate a Basic Auth `Authorization' header, and also sets the correct `ehrscapeBaseUrl' and `openehrBaseUrl` URLs.

request.description:
We will now create a new `EHR` object for a patient, normally based on the `subjectId` and `subjectNamespace` environment variables setup in your active Postman collection.

### Request body

#### ehr_status object

The `ehr_status` object must be constructed correctly and passed in the body of the request.

Most of the object is boilerplate and we have setup the Pre-request Script to format this correctly for you, as well as generating a random `subjectId`.

#### subjectId

The `subjectId` is some kind of real-world identifier like a national medical identifier or hospital number.

We have setup this particular call to automatically generate a `subjectId` based on a random Guid.

#### subjectNamespace

The `subjectNamespace` is a string that just says what type of identifier is being passed in a subjectId.  
Typically this will be issued by a national authority e.g. in the UK, the namespace for an NHS number is

`https://fhir.nhs.uk/Id/nhs-number`.

> **Warning**  
There is an issue with **EhrBase** which does not allow a `subjectNamespace` with a '_' or '.' character. 
  

### Response

#### 201 Created

If successful, you will get a `201 Created` response and the `EHR` object that has been created will be returned in the Response body.

#### Retrieve the `ehrId`

The critical piece of information that you will need to retrieve is the `ehrId`.

In the the Response body, you will find this at `ehr_id.value`

```
  "ehr_id": {
        "_type": "HIER_OBJECT_ID",
        "value": "80ea197f-c222-4edc-bd46-b91afc295d49"
    },

 ```

Copy the value, and update the `ehrId` environment in Postman, so that it can be used in subsequent API calls, without having to copy it each time.

If you need guidance on how to do this, have a look at \[this short video\].([https://vimeo.com/786642900](https://vimeo.com/786642900))

### Next Steps

Now that we have successfully registered the person with the CDR by creating an `EHR` object for them, let's see what happens if we try to create a another `EHR` objet for the same person.

request.description:
Now we will call the same **Create EHR** call again with the same `subjectId` and `subjectNamespace`.

### Response

You will see that it returns a `409 Conflict` error.

```json
{
    "error": "Conflict",
    "message": "Specified party has already an EHR set (partyId=4844a993-208d-472d-8f97-cc0beff6f07a)"
}
```

This is correct as a given subjectID/subjectNamespace can only ever be associated with a single `EHR`.

### Next steps

We will now use the `GET /ehr` request to fetch the EHR object we have just created.

item.description:
Now that we have checked that we are correctly connected to our CDR of choice, we will register a new patient with the CDR.

By design, we try to minimise any identifiable demographic carried in the CDR, and inside the CDR, the patient is uniquely identified by a GUID, known as the `ehrId`. Patient name, address, Date of birth etc are not normally carried in the CDR but in an external demographics service.

To register a new patient with the CDR we need to create an `EHR` object for them, which will  allocate the `ehrId` for that patient, which we will use to access their records.

There are 2 approaches to creating a new `EHR` object.

1. Most commonly the POST /ehr call is used, passing in an external real-world identifier such as a national health identifier e.g. an NHS Number `subjectId`.

2. Less commonly, an existing `ehrId`, generated by an external service is used to create the `EHR` object via a PUT /ehr call.

We will use the first option - POST /ehr for this example.

request.description:
To fetch a patient's `EHR` object from the CDR, we pass the `subjectId` and `subjectNamespace` as parameters as a `GET /ehr` request.

When you run this request, these parameters will be pre-populated automatically from your Postman environment.

### Response

If the request is successful, you should get `200 OK`  and you will see `EHR` object appear in Response Body.

The key piece of information you need to extract from this object is the `ehrId` which is at `ehr_id.value`.

It will be  a *Guid* like "4ea322b1-3bc9-4a1e-8652-fb43c739a793".

When developing a real app you would likely cache the `ehrId` you will use it for almost every call to a patient record.

To simulate this here, copy the 'ehrId' value and update the Postman ehrID environment variable. This will let you pre-populate the next set of requests where they need the `ehrId`.

If Postman is new to you, [this short video](video).

item.description:
Now that we have registered the patient and created their 'EHR' object, how do fetch that object back?

Typically when you are building an app you will know the patients real-word identifier but will not store their `ehrId` externally. 

You will need to know the `ehrId` to work with the patient's record, so typically you will first run a `GET /ehr` request to fetch the patient's `EHR` object and extract the `ehrId`.

                <term_definitions code="at0001">
                    <items id="text">History</items>
                    <items id="description">History Structural node.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0003">
                    <items id="text">blood pressure</items>
                    <items id="description">@ internal @</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0004">
                    <items id="text">Systolic</items>
                    <items id="description">Peak systemic arterial blood pressure  - measured in systolic or contraction phase of the heart cycle.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0005">
                    <items id="text">Diastolic</items>
                    <items id="description">Minimum systemic arterial blood pressure - measured in the diastolic or relaxation phase of the heart cycle.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0006">
                    <items id="text">Any event</items>
                    <items id="description">Default, unspecified point in time or interval event which may be explicitly defined in a template or at run-time.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0007">
                    <items id="text">state structure</items>
                    <items id="description">@ internal @</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0008">
                    <items id="text">Position</items>
                    <items id="description">The position of the individual at the time of measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0011">
                    <items id="text">Tree</items>
                    <items id="description">List structure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0013">
                    <items id="text">Cuff size</items>
                    <items id="description">The size of the cuff used for blood pressure measurement.</items>
                    <items id="comment">Perloff D, Grim C, Flack J, Frohlich ED, Hill M, McDonald M, Morgenstern BZ. Human blood pressure determination by sphygmomanometry. Circulation 1993;88;2460-2470. </items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0014">
                    <items id="text">Location of measurement</items>
                    <items id="description">Simple body site where blood pressure was measured.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0015">
                    <items id="text">Adult Thigh</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for an adult thigh.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0016">
                    <items id="text">Large Adult</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff for adults with larger arms.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0017">
                    <items id="text">Adult</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff that is standard for an adult.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0025">
                    <items id="text">Right arm</items>
                    <items id="description">The right arm of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0026">
                    <items id="text">Left arm</items>
                    <items id="description">The left arm of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0027">
                    <items id="text">Right thigh</items>
                    <items id="description">The right thigh of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0028">
                    <items id="text">Left thigh</items>
                    <items id="description">The left thigh of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0033">
                    <items id="text">Comment</items>
                    <items id="description">Additional narrative about the measurement, not captured in other fields.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1000">
                    <items id="text">Standing</items>
                    <items id="description">Standing at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1001">
                    <items id="text">Sitting</items>
                    <items id="description">Sitting (for example on bed or chair) at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1002">
                    <items id="text">Reclining</items>
                    <items id="description">Reclining at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1003">
                    <items id="text">Lying</items>
                    <items id="description">Lying flat at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1005">
                    <items id="text">Tilt</items>
                    <items id="description">The craniocaudal tilt of the surface on which the person is lying at the time of measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1006">
                    <items id="text">Mean arterial pressure</items>
                    <items id="description">The average arterial pressure that occurs over the entire course of the heart contraction and relaxation cycle.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1007">
                    <items id="text">Pulse pressure</items>
                    <items id="description">The difference between the systolic and diastolic pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1008">
                    <items id="text">Small Adult</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for a small adult.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1009">
                    <items id="text">Paediatric/Child</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff that is appropriate for a child or adult with a thin arm.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1010">
                    <items id="text">Diastolic endpoint</items>
                    <items id="description">Record which Korotkoff sound is used for determining diastolic pressure using auscultative method.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1011">
                    <items id="text">Phase IV</items>
                    <items id="description">The fourth Korotkoff sound is identified as an abrupt muffling of sounds.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1012">
                    <items id="text">Phase V</items>
                    <items id="description">The fifth Korotkoff sound is identified by absence of sounds as the cuff pressure drops below the diastolic blood pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1014">
                    <items id="text">Lying with tilt to left</items>
                    <items id="description">Lying flat with some lateral tilt, usually angled towards the left side.   Commonly required in the last trimester of pregnancy to relieve aortocaval compression.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1018">
                    <items id="text">Infant</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for infants.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1019">
                    <items id="text">Neonatal</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for a neonate, assuming cuff is the appropriate size for maturity and birthweight of the neonate.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1020">
                    <items id="text">Right wrist</items>
                    <items id="description">The right wrist of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1021">
                    <items id="text">Left wrist</items>
                    <items id="description">The left wrist of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1025">
                    <items id="text">Device</items>
                    <items id="description">Details about sphygmomanometer or other device used to measure the blood pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1026">
                    <items id="text">Right ankle</items>
                    <items id="description">The right ankle of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1030">
                    <items id="text">Exertion</items>
                    <items id="description">Details about physical activity undertaken at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1031">
                    <items id="text">Left ankle</items>
                    <items id="description">The left ankle of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1032">
                    <items id="text">Finger</items>
                    <items id="description">A finger of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1035">
                    <items id="text">Method</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measurement of blood pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1036">
                    <items id="text">Auscultation</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measuring blood pressure externally, using a stethoscope and Korotkoff sounds.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1037">
                    <items id="text">Palpation</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measuring blood pressure externally, using palpation (usually of the brachial or radial arteries).</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1038">
                    <items id="text">Mean arterial pressure formula</items>
                    <items id="description">Formula used to calculate the Mean Arterial Pressure (if recorded in data).</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1039">
                    <items id="text">Machine</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measuring blood pressure externally, using a blood pressure machine.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1040">
                    <items id="text">Invasive</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measuring blood pressure internally ie involving penetration of the skin and measuring inside blood vessels.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1042">
                    <items id="text">24 hour average</items>
                    <items id="description">Estimate of the average blood pressure over a 24 hour period.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1043">
                    <items id="text">Sleep status</items>
                    <items id="description">Sleep status - supports interpretation of 24 hour ambulatory blood pressure records.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1044">
                    <items id="text">Awake</items>
                    <items id="description">The individual is fully conscious.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1045">
                    <items id="text">Sleeping</items>
                    <items id="description">The individual is in the natural state of bodily rest.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1051">
                    <items id="text">Toe</items>
                    <items id="description">A toe of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1052">
                    <items id="text">Confounding factors</items>
                    <items id="description">Comment on and record other incidental factors that may be contributing to the blood pressure measurement.  For example, level of anxiety or 'white coat syndrome'; pain or fever; changes in atmospheric pressure etc.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1053">
                    <items id="text">Intra-arterial</items>
                    <items id="description">Invasive measurement via transducer access line within an artery.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1054">
                    <items id="text">Systolic pressure formula</items>
                    <items id="description">Formula used to calculate the systolic pressure from from mean arterial pressure (if recorded in data).</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1055">
                    <items id="text">Diastolic pressure formula</items>
                    <items id="description">Formula used to calculate the diastolic pressure from mean arterial pressure (if recorded in data).</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1057">
                    <items id="text">Structured measurement location</items>
                    <items id="description">Structured anatomical location of where the measurement was taken.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1058">
                    <items id="text">Extension</items>
                    <items id="description">Additional information required to capture local context or to align with other reference models/formalisms.</items>
                    <items id="comment">For example: Local hospital departmental infomation or additional metadata to align with FHIR or CIMI equivalents.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1059">
                    <items id="text">Clinical interpretation</items>
                    <items id="description">Single word, phrase or brief description that represents the clinical meaning and significance of the blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1056">
                    <items id="text">Dorsum of foot</items>
                    <items id="description">The individual's dorsum of the foot.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0000">

request.description:
The POST `/template` request uploads and registers an `Operational template`, often called an OPT file, with the CDR.

This is an XML file normally with a `.opt` extension which contains all of the constraint information needed to validate openEHR object instance data when it is committed as a `Composition` object.

It is generated automatically and exported by openEHR modelling tools such as [Archetype Designer](https://tools.openehr.org/designer/#/)

This template represents a simple dataset used to underpin a data-entry form for a simple 'GP Annual review' which includes height, weight and blood pressure recordings.

Although readily parsable, it is designed to be machine-readable and can be hard to navigate. 

Later we will explore the **'JSON Web template'** format as an alternative (actually derived from the .OPT) which is much easier to navigate and parse.

#### 201 Created

If the template uploads successfully you should get a `201 Created` response and the uploaded XML structure will be mirrored back in the Response body.

The template contains a `template_id`, which you will need to know to be able to save clinical data via a `Composition` object.

We have set Postman to have automatically updated the `template_id` in your Postman environment, so that you do not have to re-type it.

#### 409 Conflict error

In EhrBase, if you try to re-upload a template, you will get a `409 Conflict` error. 
```json
{
    "error": "Conflict",
    "message": "Operational template with this template ID already exists: GP - Annual Review"
}
```

In production this is correct behaviour, as uploading a template with breaking changes can cause significant issues to existing data. For this reason EhrBase forces you to make template overwrites via a separate [Admin API](https://ehrbase.readthedocs.io/en/latest/03_development/07_admin/index.html)

You can also allow template overwrites in the EhrBase environment settings.

>**Note**
>The .env setting in Ehrbase to disable this behaviour for development is
>`SYSTEM_ALLOW_TEMPLATE_OVERWRITE=true`

This can be helpful when working in dev environment where templates are in development. The BetterCDR allows template overwrites by default.

### Next steps:

Now that we have registered this template with the CDR we will show how to upload some actual Annual GP Review patient data to the CDR via a `Composition` object.

                <term_definitions code="at0001">
                    <items id="text">History</items>

                <term_definitions code="at0003">
                    <items id="text">blood pressure</items>
                    <items id="description">@ internal @</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0004">
                    <items id="text">Systolic</items>
                    <items id="description">Peak systemic arterial blood pressure  - measured in systolic or contraction phase of the heart cycle.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0005">
                    <items id="text">Diastolic</items>
                    <items id="description">Minimum systemic arterial blood pressure - measured in the diastolic or relaxation phase of the heart cycle.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0006">
                    <items id="text">Any event</items>
                    <items id="description">Default, unspecified point in time or interval event which may be explicitly defined in a template or at run-time.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0007">
                    <items id="text">state structure</items>
                    <items id="description">@ internal @</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0008">
                    <items id="text">Position</items>
                    <items id="description">The position of the individual at the time of measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0011">
                    <items id="text">Tree</items>
                    <items id="description">List structure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0013">
                    <items id="text">Cuff size</items>
                    <items id="description">The size of the cuff used for blood pressure measurement.</items>
                    <items id="comment">Perloff D, Grim C, Flack J, Frohlich ED, Hill M, McDonald M, Morgenstern BZ. Human blood pressure determination by sphygmomanometry. Circulation 1993;88;2460-2470. </items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0014">
                    <items id="text">Location of measurement</items>
                    <items id="description">Simple body site where blood pressure was measured.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0015">
                    <items id="text">Adult Thigh</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for an adult thigh.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0016">
                    <items id="text">Large Adult</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff for adults with larger arms.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0017">
                    <items id="text">Adult</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff that is standard for an adult.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0025">
                    <items id="text">Right arm</items>
                    <items id="description">The right arm of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0026">
                    <items id="text">Left arm</items>
                    <items id="description">The left arm of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0027">
                    <items id="text">Right thigh</items>
                    <items id="description">The right thigh of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0028">
                    <items id="text">Left thigh</items>
                    <items id="description">The left thigh of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0033">
                    <items id="text">Comment</items>
                    <items id="description">Additional narrative about the measurement, not captured in other fields.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1000">
                    <items id="text">Standing</items>
                    <items id="description">Standing at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1001">
                    <items id="text">Sitting</items>
                    <items id="description">Sitting (for example on bed or chair) at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1002">
                    <items id="text">Reclining</items>
                    <items id="description">Reclining at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1003">
                    <items id="text">Lying</items>
                    <items id="description">Lying flat at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1005">
                    <items id="text">Tilt</items>
                    <items id="description">The craniocaudal tilt of the surface on which the person is lying at the time of measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1006">
                    <items id="text">Mean arterial pressure</items>
                    <items id="description">The average arterial pressure that occurs over the entire course of the heart contraction and relaxation cycle.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1007">
                    <items id="text">Pulse pressure</items>
                    <items id="description">The difference between the systolic and diastolic pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1008">
                    <items id="text">Small Adult</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for a small adult.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1009">
                    <items id="text">Paediatric/Child</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff that is appropriate for a child or adult with a thin arm.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1010">
                    <items id="text">Diastolic endpoint</items>
                    <items id="description">Record which Korotkoff sound is used for determining diastolic pressure using auscultative method.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1011">
                    <items id="text">Phase IV</items>
                    <items id="description">The fourth Korotkoff sound is identified as an abrupt muffling of sounds.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1012">
                    <items id="text">Phase V</items>
                    <items id="description">The fifth Korotkoff sound is identified by absence of sounds as the cuff pressure drops below the diastolic blood pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1014">
                    <items id="text">Lying with tilt to left</items>
                    <items id="description">Lying flat with some lateral tilt, usually angled towards the left side.   Commonly required in the last trimester of pregnancy to relieve aortocaval compression.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1018">
                    <items id="text">Infant</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for infants.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1019">
                    <items id="text">Neonatal</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for a neonate, assuming cuff is the appropriate size for maturity and birthweight of the neonate.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1020">
                    <items id="text">Right wrist</items>
                    <items id="description">The right wrist of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1021">
                    <items id="text">Left wrist</items>
                    <items id="description">The left wrist of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1025">
                    <items id="text">Device</items>
                    <items id="description">Details about sphygmomanometer or other device used to measure the blood pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1026">
                    <items id="text">Right ankle</items>
                    <items id="description">The right ankle of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1030">
                    <items id="text">Exertion</items>
                    <items id="description">Details about physical activity undertaken at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1031">
                    <items id="text">Left ankle</items>
                    <items id="description">The left ankle of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1032">
                    <items id="text">Finger</items>
                    <items id="description">A finger of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1035">
                    <items id="text">Method</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measurement of blood pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1036">
                    <items id="text">Auscultation</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measuring blood pressure externally, using a stethoscope and Korotkoff sounds.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1037">
                    <items id="text">Palpation</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measuring blood pressure externally, using palpation (usually of the brachial or radial arteries).</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1038">
                    <items id="text">Mean arterial pressure formula</items>
                    <items id="description">Formula used to calculate the Mean Arterial Pressure (if recorded in data).</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1039">
                    <items id="text">Machine</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measuring blood pressure externally, using a blood pressure machine.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1040">
                    <items id="text">Invasive</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measuring blood pressure internally ie involving penetration of the skin and measuring inside blood vessels.</items>

                <term_definitions code="at0001">
                    <items id="text">History</items>
                    <items id="description">History Structural node.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0003">
                    <items id="text">blood pressure</items>
                    <items id="description">@ internal @</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0004">
                    <items id="text">Systolic</items>
                    <items id="description">Peak systemic arterial blood pressure  - measured in systolic or contraction phase of the heart cycle.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0005">
                    <items id="text">Diastolic</items>
                    <items id="description">Minimum systemic arterial blood pressure - measured in the diastolic or relaxation phase of the heart cycle.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0006">
                    <items id="text">Any event</items>
                    <items id="description">Default, unspecified point in time or interval event which may be explicitly defined in a template or at run-time.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0007">
                    <items id="text">state structure</items>
                    <items id="description">@ internal @</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0008">
                    <items id="text">Position</items>
                    <items id="description">The position of the individual at the time of measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0011">
                    <items id="text">Tree</items>
                    <items id="description">List structure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0013">
                    <items id="text">Cuff size</items>
                    <items id="description">The size of the cuff used for blood pressure measurement.</items>
                    <items id="comment">Perloff D, Grim C, Flack J, Frohlich ED, Hill M, McDonald M, Morgenstern BZ. Human blood pressure determination by sphygmomanometry. Circulation 1993;88;2460-2470. </items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0014">
                    <items id="text">Location of measurement</items>
                    <items id="description">Simple body site where blood pressure was measured.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0015">
                    <items id="text">Adult Thigh</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for an adult thigh.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0016">
                    <items id="text">Large Adult</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff for adults with larger arms.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0017">
                    <items id="text">Adult</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff that is standard for an adult.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0025">
                    <items id="text">Right arm</items>
                    <items id="description">The right arm of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0026">
                    <items id="text">Left arm</items>
                    <items id="description">The left arm of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0027">
                    <items id="text">Right thigh</items>
                    <items id="description">The right thigh of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0028">
                    <items id="text">Left thigh</items>
                    <items id="description">The left thigh of the person.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at0033">
                    <items id="text">Comment</items>
                    <items id="description">Additional narrative about the measurement, not captured in other fields.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1000">
                    <items id="text">Standing</items>
                    <items id="description">Standing at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1001">
                    <items id="text">Sitting</items>
                    <items id="description">Sitting (for example on bed or chair) at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1002">
                    <items id="text">Reclining</items>
                    <items id="description">Reclining at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1003">
                    <items id="text">Lying</items>
                    <items id="description">Lying flat at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1005">
                    <items id="text">Tilt</items>
                    <items id="description">The craniocaudal tilt of the surface on which the person is lying at the time of measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1006">
                    <items id="text">Mean arterial pressure</items>
                    <items id="description">The average arterial pressure that occurs over the entire course of the heart contraction and relaxation cycle.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1007">
                    <items id="text">Pulse pressure</items>
                    <items id="description">The difference between the systolic and diastolic pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1008">
                    <items id="text">Small Adult</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for a small adult.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1009">
                    <items id="text">Paediatric/Child</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff that is appropriate for a child or adult with a thin arm.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1010">
                    <items id="text">Diastolic endpoint</items>
                    <items id="description">Record which Korotkoff sound is used for determining diastolic pressure using auscultative method.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1011">
                    <items id="text">Phase IV</items>
                    <items id="description">The fourth Korotkoff sound is identified as an abrupt muffling of sounds.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1012">
                    <items id="text">Phase V</items>
                    <items id="description">The fifth Korotkoff sound is identified by absence of sounds as the cuff pressure drops below the diastolic blood pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1014">
                    <items id="text">Lying with tilt to left</items>
                    <items id="description">Lying flat with some lateral tilt, usually angled towards the left side.   Commonly required in the last trimester of pregnancy to relieve aortocaval compression.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1018">
                    <items id="text">Infant</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for infants.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1019">
                    <items id="text">Neonatal</items>
                    <items id="description">A cuff used for a neonate, assuming cuff is the appropriate size for maturity and birthweight of the neonate.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1020">
                    <items id="text">Right wrist</items>
                    <items id="description">The right wrist of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1021">
                    <items id="text">Left wrist</items>
                    <items id="description">The left wrist of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1025">
                    <items id="text">Device</items>
                    <items id="description">Details about sphygmomanometer or other device used to measure the blood pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1026">
                    <items id="text">Right ankle</items>
                    <items id="description">The right ankle of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1030">
                    <items id="text">Exertion</items>
                    <items id="description">Details about physical activity undertaken at the time of blood pressure measurement.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1031">
                    <items id="text">Left ankle</items>
                    <items id="description">The left ankle of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1032">
                    <items id="text">Finger</items>
                    <items id="description">A finger of the individual.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1035">
                    <items id="text">Method</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measurement of blood pressure.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1036">
                    <items id="text">Auscultation</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measuring blood pressure externally, using a stethoscope and Korotkoff sounds.</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1037">
                    <items id="text">Palpation</items>
                    <items id="description">Method of measuring blood pressure externally, using palpation (usually of the brachial or radial arteries).</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1038">
                    <items id="text">Mean arterial pressure formula</items>
                    <items id="description">Formula used to calculate the Mean Arterial Pressure (if recorded in data).</items>
                </term_definitions>
                <term_definitions code="at1039">
                    <items id="text">Machine</items>

request.description: Retreive a list of openEHR Templates currently registered on the CDR.
Down load an ADL 1.4 template from the CDR.

Returns an openEhr template in its web-appropriate representation (as a JSON object). 

A note on languages: the web template will be generated with localized names for all the languages that the underlying template supports, unless it is specified differently via the defaultLanguage and languages query parameters, both of which are optional. 

The defaultLanguage parameter determines the default name for each web template node (the localizedName property), whereas the languages parameter will generate additional localized names inside the localizedNames map for all the languages listed in this parameter (different languages should be separated by a comma: en,sl,no). 

Note that the underlying openEhr template needs to support these languages, or else a 400 error (bad request) will be returned (TMPL-3061).

item.description:
Having ensured that the connection to the CDR is working correctly, we will now upload an openEHR template definition to the CDR.

A template is how the CDR 'knows' about new data models, without any need for the internal database inside to be re-engineered.

The template also acts as a validation layer in the same way as a database schema in enforcing rules and constraints in the data e.g making some items mandatory, enforcing numeric ranges or allowed coded values.

For now, don't worry about how these template files are created. This work is generally done by clinical/care informaticians, using specialised tools like the [openEHR Archetype Designer](https://tools.openehr.org/designer/#/), and without any need for programming/engineering input. 

This video explains the data modelling process for a Care Home dataset.
 
[![openEHR Archetypes and Templates](https://i.vimeocdn.com/video/1173356544_130x73)](https://player.vimeo.com/video/567491615)

request.description:
## Ehrscape POST /composition (FLAT)

> **Note**  
Note that this request uses the Ehrscape service and not the openEHR REST service. 
  

### Request

This request `POST /composition`, submits a new openEHR composition to the specified patient `EHR`.

#### ehrId:

The `ehrId` of patient `EHR` into which the composition should be committed.

#### templateID:

The `templateId` of the template against which the composition must be validated.

#### committerName (optional):

An optional name of the person responsible for making the commit. Normally drawn from the user login.

#### format:

The composition can be in one of the supported formats (FLAT, STRUCTURED, RAW or TDD). We will use the 'FLAT' format for this example. We will cover the alternative formats later

### Response

##### Successfully created

The Response body will contain a link to the newly created composition and the unique `compositionUid` which is assigned to the composition by the CDR.

``` json
{
    "meta": {
        "href": {
            "url": "http://165.227.231.224:8080/ehrbase/rest/ecis/v1/composition?ehrId=700d884e-324a-4060-9783-28a805a65c5a&templateId=GP - Annual Review&committerName=Dr Franke&format=FLAT/rest/ecis/v1/composition/dcdfa691-2827-4516-b3d9-005ff6475d07::local.ehrbase.org::1"
        }
    },
    "action": "CREATE",
    "compositionUid": "dcdfa691-2827-4516-b3d9-005ff6475d07::local.ehrbase.org::1"
}

 ```

##### 400 Bad request

A variety of problems may produce this error but the most common is invalid composition data e.g A missing mandatory element or data value not in range.

##### 401 Unauthenticated

The user could not be authenticated.

##### Forbidden

The user does not have the required permissions to execute this request.

##### 404 Not found

An EHR with the given ID does not exist or a Template with the given ID does not exist.

#### compositionUid

The `compositionUid` in the Response is needed if you wish to retrieve a composition directly.

You will see that it is a 3 part identifier.

`"dcdfa691-2827-4516-b3d9-005ff6475d07::local.ehrbase.org::1"`

The first part is just a uniqueGUID, the second is the namespace defined by the CDR, and the third is a **version suffix**.

If you need to update a composition, its suffix is incremented automatically by the CDR via a `PUT / composition` call.

##### Update compositionId

Make sure you now update your your `compositionId` Postman environment variable with the value of `compositionUid`.

Note that the Postman variable is called `compositionId` and **not** `compositonUid`

If you need guidance on how to do this, have a look at \[this short video\].([https://vimeo.com/786642900](https://vimeo.com/786642900)).

### Next steps

Now that we have committed our first composition, we will fetch it back.

request.description:
Returns an openEHR composition denoted by the specified ID in one of the supported formats, along with some metadata.

The ID can be specified as a complete unique ID with the domain and version part (8849182c-82ad-4088-a07f-48ead4180515::ehrscape.com::1), or just the identifier part (8849182c-82ad-4088-a07f-48ead4180515), in which case the last version of the composition will be returned.

##### Response codes
```
200	Success - returns composition data and meta-data in response body.	
204	No content - requested composition has been deleted. In this case, the HTTP response will contain a Link header giving the URL to the last active (non-deleted) version of the composition.
400	Could not parse the format parameter (COMP-1011).
401	Unauthenticated - could not authenticate the user (SYS-9401).
403	Forbidden - the user does not have the required permissions to execute this request (SYS-9403).
404	Composition with the given ID does not exist (COMP-1021).
```

item.description:
Now that we have uploaded the 'GP Annual Review' template, let's imagine that the GP Annual Review app looks a little like this..

!(IMAGE)

The job of the developer is to hook up the UI to create a JSON or XML object with a very specific structure, called a `Composition`.

The exact shape of that structure is based on the openEHR Reference model and the template definition which profiles it for the 'Annual GP Review' use case.

The CDR will validate the submitted JSON against the template and will raise an error if it finds any discrepancies or data values that are not within the allowed constraints.

In this way it is works like any traditional database, rejecting any erroneous or invalid data.

For this section, initially we will switch to using the Ehrscape API, rather than the openEHR REST API, as it fully supports the FLAT and STRUCTURED forms of JSON Composition. These

The openEHR REST API is being adapted to support these formats but support in production CDRs remains incomplete.

Conceptually, the openEHR REST API version of /composition is identical.

request.description:
Saves a new openEHR composition to the specified patient EHR sing the Mental Health template.

The composition can be in one of the supported formats (FLAT, STRUCTURED, RAW or TDD). Unless the `format` parameter is RAW, the `templateId` parameter is required. 

The composition data is sent in the request body.

EHR ID: The EHR to save the composition into, needs to be specified via the `ehrId` parameter.

You will note that the structure of the composition body is quite different to that of the GP Annual review. All of the complexity of creating and retrieving openEHR data is in understanding the 'shape' of tis object and its constraints.

We will show you the best approaches to that problem later.
  
##### Response Messages
```
201	Successfully created - response body will contain a link to the newly created composition	
400	Bad request - could not parse the format parameter (COMP-1011), templateId not specified (TMPL-3031), no EHR to save to can be determined (EHR-2031), composition language and territory problems (COMP-1051, COMP-1061, COMP-1071), invalid composition data (COMP-1081).
401	Unauthenticated - could not authenticate the user (SYS-9401).
403	Forbidden - the user does not have the required permissions to execute this request (SYS-9403).
404	EHR with the given ID does not exist (EHR-2021), template with the given ID does not exist (TMPL-3021).
```

request.description:
## Ehrscape GET /composition (FLAT)

This example returns an openEHR composition denoted by the specified `compositionId` in `FLAT OUTPUT` format, along with some metadata.

### Request

### Headers

The `content-type` header is set to `application/json`.

#### compositionId

The `compositionId` can be specified as a complete unique ID with the domain and version part (8849182c-82ad-4088-a07f-48ead4180515::ehrscape.com::1),

or just the identifier part (8849182c-82ad-4088-a07f-48ead4180515), in which case the last version of the composition will be returned.

If you correctly saved the Postman `compositionId` variable in the last section, this should be picked up.

#### format

The `format` parameter is set to `FLAT`. This will return a `FLAT OUTPUT` json composition structure.

### Response

The Response returns a Composition in  `FLAT OUTPUT` json composition structure. 

##### Response codes
```
200	Success - returns composition data and meta-data in response body

204	No content - requested composition has been deleted. In this case, the HTTP response will contain a Link header giving the URL to the last active (non-deleted) version of the composition.

400	Could not parse the format parameter 

401	Unauthenticated - could not authenticate the user 

403	Forbidden - the user does not have the required permissions to execute this request 

404	Composition with the given ID does not exist
```

### Next steps

In the next section we will look at another Ehrscape format, `STRUCTURED` json.

request.description:
## Ehrscape GET /composition (STRUCTURED)

This example returns the same openEHR composition denoted by the specified `compositionId` but in `STRUCTURED OUTPUT` format, along with some metadata.

We will discuss the different Composition  formats later but the choice is mostly down to personal preference.

### Request Headers

The `content-type` header is set to `application/json`.

### Request Parameters

#### compositionId

The `compositionId` can be specified as a complete unique ID with the domain and version part (8849182c-82ad-4088-a07f-48ead4180515::ehrscape.com::1),

or just the identifier part (8849182c-82ad-4088-a07f-48ead4180515), in which case the last version of the composition will be returned.

If you correctly saved the Postman `compositionId` variable in the last section, this should be picked up.

#### format

The `format` parameter is set to `STRUCTURED`. This will return a `STRUCTURED OUTPUT` json composition structure.

### Response

The Response returns a Composition in  `STRUCTURED OUTPUT` json composition structure. 

##### Response codes
```
200	Success - returns composition data and meta-data in response body

204	No content - requested composition has been deleted. In this case, the HTTP response will contain a Link header giving the URL to the last active (non-deleted) version of the composition.

400	Could not parse the format parameter 

401	Unauthenticated - could not authenticate the user 

403	Forbidden - the user does not have the required permissions to execute this request 

404	Composition with the given ID does not exist
```

### Next steps

In the next section we will look at the `RAW` xml format.

item.description:
To get you started, we will start by showing how to 

1. Check the connection/authorisation to the CDR by fetching a list of any openEHR templates currently registered with the CDR, via a `GET /template` call.

2. Upload a new openEHR Template to the CDR via an XML `.opt` definition file via a `POST /template` call

3. Fetch the internal openEHR patient identifier, the `ehrId` for an example patient record already stored in the CDR via a `POST /ehr` call, by passing in their `subjectId`. This is normally an national regional identifier such as an NHS Number, or a hospital number.

4. Once the correct `ehrId` is known for the patient, you can commit an openEHR `Composition` object to the CDR using  a `POST /composition` call.

5. Fetch the whole Composition object you have just committed by running a GET /composition call, using the unique identifier allocated when it was committed.

6. Run an `AQL` (Archetype Query Language) call as `POST /query`, which fetches a more granular part of the Composition.

item.description:
This Tutorial will take you through key aspects of working with a compliant openEHR datastore, normally called a Clinical Data Repository (CDR), via the formal [openEHR REST API](https://specifications.openehr.org/releases/ITS-REST/latest), and the [Better Ehrscape API](https://www.ehrscape.com/api-explorer.html).

A `CDR` is essentially a high-performance, patient/citizen datastore, compliant with the openEHR specifications, Critically, it is a no-code ecosystem which allows data models (archetypes and templates) defined directly by care professionals, to be deployed without any database re-factoring.

1. **Getting started**: This section will quickly take you through the process of uploading a new data definition, storing data against that definition, then querying it back again.

2. **In more depth**: This section will take you through the openEHR REST API resource calls in more detail, and explain the various data formats that are supported.

## Postman features

This collection makes use of a number of Postman features which may be helpful to understand.

### Environments 

You can switch between different CDR environments. A number of the API calls automatically update useful environment variables such as the last templateId or most recent compositionId.

If you want to create your own environment, we suggest you duplicate one of the existing ones, then check or reset

-`cdrProduct`: Better|ehrBase
- `openEhrBaseUrl`: The url to the openEHR API
- `ehrscapeBaseUrl`: The url to the Ehrscape API
- `Username`: The username from which to generate a Basic Auth string.
- `Password`: The password from which to generate a Basic Auth string.


### Authorisation Helper

Authorisation is set to `Basic Auth` and is automatically inherited from the Authorisation Helper of the whole Collection. This is turn is calculated from the `Username` and `Password` variables in the active environment.

### Postman scripting

A number of the API calls reference custom Javascript code in their `Pre-Request` and `Test` tabs. Often these in turn reference 'global' utility functions in the **Collection Pre-request** tab. 

As well as allowing re-use of simple functions e.g. to extract identifiers from Response Headers, in some places this is helpful to act as *'shims'* where there are small differences in behaviours between different openEHR CDR products.

You might find some of these code snippets helpful in understanding how to create your own code to handle the various responses.

item.name: B. Reference material
Template validation constraints
item.description:
# Understanding composition Constraints and validation


As it is committed, the data will be validated against both the appropriate openEHR template and the underlying Reference Model schema.

If the data is valid, it will be stored in the CDR and is allocated a unique `compositionID`, which is returned by the POST /composition call on a successful call.

One of the key challenges in working with openEHR, is in understanding the complexities of the various datatypes and the other validation rules that apply for any particular template.

The constraint and validation rules are applied in by

1. The Reference model

2. Archetype-level constraints

3. Template-level constraints


### How to figure out which constraints apply?

As an example, I know that a particular coded entry list (perhaps drop-down) allows only a fixed selection of possible answers, which are probably coded ( a good example being a PROMS score). Where can I find how these are defined?

The ultimate source of truth is the `.opt` 'Operational template' which is uploaded to the CDR. It is essentially an aggregation of all the archetype constraints, and any local template constraints, which are then applied to the underlying RM to give the full validation target.

The .opt is a faithful representation of the underlying in-memory objects but is a pretty difficult beast to parse and understand.

Fortunately Better provide a 'web template' utility which generates a JSON version of the validation statement but in a much more understandable format -both for human consumption and parsing. The web template facility is available both from the Ehrscape API, and as an export option from the openEHR Archetype Designer.

Web templates examples will be provided for each template in the project.

item.name: Key openEHR RM attributes
item.description:
The openEHR Reference model defines a relatively small set of information model constructs which openEHR back-ends must support. This includes a number of generic classes and datatypes.

The Reference model contains virtually no clinical content e.g concepts for Medication, or Diagnosis. These are defined and managed separately as `archetypes`.

A number of key data points need to be populated in an openEHR composition, which may not be apparent from the archetypes or templates.
Developers can largely use the example instance documents and APIs for guidance but these notes may give useful background in addition to viewing the [UML view of the openEHR reference model.](http://www.openehr.org/local/releases/1.0.1/uml/index.html)

## *committer*

This is the name of the person physically committing the document ie.
the person logged on to the account. If omitted from API calls, Ehrscape
will use the domain login name.

## *composition/composer*

This is the clinical author of the document i.e the person with clinical
responsibility. Ehrscape FLAT and STRCTURTED formats handle this as
`composer_name`.

## *composition/context/start\_time*

This is the time that the clinical interaction with the patient began.
Ehrscape FLAT and STRUCTURED formats handle this as ctx/time.

## *composition/context/health\_care\_facility*

This is the healthcare facility / oragnisation under who’s remit the
encounter took place.

## *observation/time*

This is the time that a patient’s signs and symptoms were observed or a
test was run. It is set automatically by the value of the ctx/time
attribute. If you need to set the time of a specific observation you can
use

The Ehrscape FLAT and STRUCTURED formats hide much of the complexity of
these attributes, providing sensible defaults. In particular the `ctx`
header common to both JSON STRUCTURED and FLAT formats, considerably
simplifies the composition header …

request.description:
Returns an openEHR template in its web-appropriate representation (as a JSON object).

A note on languages: the web template will be generated with localized names for all the languages that the underlying template supports, unless it is specified differently via the defaultLanguage and languages query parameters, both of which are optional.

The defaultLanguage parameter determines the default name for each web template node (the localizedName property), whereas the languages parameter will generate additional localized names inside the localizedNames map for all the languages listed in this parameter (different languages should be separated by a comma: en,sl,no).

Note that the underlying openEHR template needs to support these languages, or else a 400 error (bad request) will be returned (TMPL-3061).
